ny_f_lake_george_region.blurb: The Lake George Region is a scatter of cliffs and boulders around the lake in the Adirondacks of New York, close to a lively tourist town. Trad leads, with sport not far behind, plus a modest bouldering scene and a few top-rope lines. Grades start at easy fives and reach into the 5.13s, though most of the climbing falls between 5.8 and 5.11. Shelving Rock is the largest venue: a cliff on the east side of the lake with big views, a short walk in, and a blend of modern trad and bolted lines, where some walls take direct sun and others stay shaded. Rogers Rock adds longer multi-pitch outings, and Potash Cliff and New Buck round out the sport and trad options. The season is long. Late spring and fall are the best times, early spring can leave some cliffs seeping, and summer is warm but manageable.

bc_mamquam_fsr.blurb: A string of crags along a forest road that heads east just north of the Stawamus Chief, near Squamish, British Columbia. Sport makes up the larger share and trad is close behind, with a sprinkling of boulders and top-rope lines. The grades run stiff: very few lines sit below 5.10, and the bulk fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with a handful of 5.13s. Fern Hill, The Courtyard and The Playground carry the bolted lines, while Slhanay, Top Shelf and The Longhouse are the main trad walls, some with multi-pitch routes. Slhanay and Top Shelf are shady, which makes them handy on hot summer days. Top Shelf is a crack-focused wall that is steeper than it looks, so expect a pump. Climbers who want easy routes will find few of them here.

co_staunton_rocks.blurb: Staunton Rocks is the main climbing zone of Staunton State Park in the South Platte region of Colorado, sitting at roughly 8,500 feet. It was the park's first developed climbing area and still holds the most routes. Sport dominates, with a solid block of trad plus some top-rope lines and a couple of boulder problems. The grades spread from easy fives into the 5.13s, with the heaviest concentration around 5.10 and a good number of 5.8 to 5.9 and 5.11 to 5.12 options. The terrain is a group of separate formations, among them Meadow Dome, The Dungeon, Park View Dome and Marmot Tower. Meadow Dome offers vertical faces that stay cool in summer, along with slabby south-facing walls that soak up sun and suit cooler days. The walk in is about two miles on a gentle trail.

ca_doyle_area.blurb: Doyle is a bouldering destination in northeast California, made up of two main zones: the West Face and the Fort Sage Mountains. Nearly everything here is bouldering, with only a few sport lines and a single top-rope. Grades start at the very easy end and climb to the double digits, with the great majority of problems between V0 and V5. The West Face sits in steep, rugged canyons at around 4,900 feet, with a gritty monzonite reminiscent of Joshua Tree and a wide range of problems, from short sit-starts to tall highballs with serious landings. In the Fort Sage Mountains, Rock Ridge is mostly beginner terrain with a few hard problems and some moderates, sunny and overlooking Honey Lake; east-facing blocks are in direct sun by late morning. Turtle Mountain and the Land of David add smaller clusters.

ut_white_pine_boulders.blurb: White Pine Boulders is a large concentration of boulder problems high in Little Cottonwood Canyon in Utah's Wasatch Range, and one of the busiest bouldering zones in the canyon. It is pure bouldering, with a wide spread of difficulty: plenty of V0 to V4 for newer boulderers, a deep middle band of V5 to V9, and a smaller group of hard problems up to the top end of the scale. White Pine South and White Pine North hold most of the problems, while White Pine Chutes is a talus field just down canyon from them, with mostly harder problems and some crack, arete and seam lines. Parts of the area sit in a shady aspen grove. The altitude makes this a summer area, when the lower boulder fields in the canyon become too hot.

ca_belvedere_heights_area.blurb: Belvedere Heights lies on the southwest flank of Box Springs Mountain, behind UC Riverside in Southern California. The rock is good granite, and the climbs are short. Bouldering makes up most of what is here, spread across washes and steep hillsides, with sport routes, some gear-friendly cracks and a few top-rope problems alongside. Boulder grades are mostly easy to moderate, from VB through about V3 with a few harder ones, while the roped routes center on the 5.9 to 5.10 range with a few harder lines. Many walls stand close together among smaller boulders, and the taller walls are in more remote spots that need a longer hike. Belvedere Heights Bouldering, the Main Wall and Sleepers Wall are the largest zones. Riverside often runs 10 degrees or more warmer than the high desert, so it works when other Southern California areas are cold.
